currentUse: 570 Broome, a 25-story, 54-unit luxury condominium tower (completed 2019), occupies the church site.
summary: Our Lady of Vilnius Church at 568-570 Broome Street was demolished in April 2015 — Draugas reported the demolition under way with a farewell gathering on April 26, 2015 (105 candles for the building's 105 years), and stated in 2016 that the building was 'galutinai nugriautas 2015 m. balandį' — four years after the NY Court of Appeals ruled for the archdiocese. The archdiocese sold the property to Extell Development for $13 million; Extell flipped it to SoHo Broome Condos LLC for $18.4 million in early 2014, and a residential tower permit was filed that August. Today the site holds 570 Broome, a 25-story, 54-unit condominium designed by Tahir Demircioglu (Builtd) for Agime Group, completed in 2019; the building's marketing makes no mention of the church. The parish tabernacle went to the Church of the Blessed Kateri Tekakwitha and sacramental records to St. Anthony of Padua on Sullivan Street. The parishioner-run memorial blog remains active as of May 2026, now advocating for other endangered churches such as St. Mary's in Yonkers.

developments.headline: Church demolished — April 2015, resolved by the Draugas record
developments.detail: Draugas of April 30, 2015 (pp. 1, 4, Gitana Merkelienė, 'Griaunama Aušros Vartų bažnyčia') reported the demolition under way — crosses already gone from the towers, the building 'jau beveik sulygintas su žeme' — with a farewell gathering on April 26, 2015: 105 candles for the building's 105 years. A Draugas follow-up of August 25, 2016 (p. 5) states the building was 'galutinai nugriautas 2015 m. balandį.' A June 2020 Draugas item describing demolition 'in progress' is a recycled near-verbatim reprint of the April 2015 farewell report and is not evidence of a 2020 demolition. Tabernacle had gone to Blessed Kateri Tekakwitha church, records to St. Anthony of Padua.

developments.headline: The closure and the locking, from the scanned Draugas record
developments.detail: The scanned-era Draugas issues document the closure fight in real time. The first closure report ran September 28, 2006 (BNS): the archdiocese intended to close 'the last Lithuanian house of prayer in New York.' The announcement came in two stages on January 19, 2007 — the 10 a.m. realignment list of 21 closures did not include the parish; a 5 p.m. archdiocese statement said it would close anyway. On the morning of February 26, 2007, pastor Eugene Sawicki was summoned to meet Cardinal Egan; while he was away, the locks were changed and a guard posted. No closure date had been announced, and no final Mass was ever held. Parishioners held a candlelight vigil at the locked doors that evening, filed an appeal with the Congregation for the Clergy on April 4, 2007, and delivered 396 signed petitions plus over 3,000 online statements. On April 28, 2007 Benedict XVI told President Adamkus in a private audience that he would discuss the church with the US bishops. The Sunday gatherings at the locked doors became a weekly 'virtual church' that continued for eight years, until the demolition.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The 2015-vs-2020 demolition conflict is RESOLVED: the June 2020 Draugas 'demolition in progress' item is a recycled near-verbatim reprint of the April 2015 farewell report (same 105 candles, same 'praėjusį sekmadienį' framing). Demolition = April 2015, per Draugas 2015-04-30 pp. 1, 4 and 2016-08-25 p. 5. Archive's 'sold for tens of millions' overstates the archdiocese's sale ($13M to Extell); the $18.4M flip was Extell's, not the church's.
